claim: Acetylcholine is released in visual cortex by axonal projections from the basal forebrain.
source: Acetylcholine is released in visual cortex by axonal projections from the basal forebrain.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the anatomical source of acetylcholine in visual cortex.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic axons in mouse visual cortex provide a binary locomotion state signal.
source: Using two-photon calcium imaging in behaving mice, we show that basal forebrain cholinergic axons in the mouse visual cortex provide a binary locomotion state signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Cholinergic axons in visual cortex show no evidence of responses to visual stimuli.
source: In these axons, we found no evidence of responses to visual stimuli or visuomotor prediction errors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1G-I showing no significant responses to gratings, visual flow, or visuomotor mismatch.

claim: Cholinergic axons in visual cortex show no evidence of responses to visuomotor prediction errors.
source: In these axons, we found no evidence of responses to visual stimuli or visuomotor prediction errors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1I showing no significant response to visuomotor mismatch.

claim: Optogenetic activation of cholinergic axons in visual cortex in isolation did not drive local neuronal activity.
source: While optogenetic activation of cholinergic axons in visual cortex in isolation did not drive local neuronal activity, when paired with visuomotor stimuli, it resulted in layer-specific increases of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5C-D showing no increase in calcium activity upon optogenetic stimulation alone.

claim: Optogenetic activation of cholinergic axons paired with visuomotor stimuli resulted in layer-specific increases of neuronal activity.
source: While optogenetic activation of cholinergic axons in visual cortex in isolation did not drive local neuronal activity, when paired with visuomotor stimuli, it resulted in layer-specific increases of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4 showing differential effects in layer 2/3 versus layer 5.

claim: Responses in layer 5 neurons to both top-down and bottom-up inputs were increased in amplitude by cholinergic activation.
source: Responses in layer 5 neurons to both top-down and bottom-up inputs were increased in amplitude and decreased in latency, whereas those in layer 2/3 neurons remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4D, F, H showing increased responses in layer 5 to gratings, mismatch, and locomotion onset with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Responses in layer 5 neurons to both top-down and bottom-up inputs were decreased in latency by cholinergic activation.
source: Responses in layer 5 neurons to both top-down and bottom-up inputs were increased in amplitude and decreased in latency, whereas those in layer 2/3 neurons remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7B showing decreased response latency in layer 5 neurons.

claim: Responses in layer 2/3 neurons remained unchanged with cholinergic activation.
source: Responses in layer 5 neurons to both top-down and bottom-up inputs were increased in amplitude and decreased in latency, whereas those in layer 2/3 neurons remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4C, E, G showing no significant changes in layer 2/3 responses with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Acetylcholine underlies the locomotion-associated decorrelation of activity between neurons in both layer 2/3 and layer 5.
source: Using opto- and chemogenetic manipulations of cholinergic activity, we found acetylcholine to underlie the locomotion-associated decorrelation of activity between neurons in both layer 2/3 and layer 5.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 showing decorrelation effects with optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulations.

claim: Acetylcholine augments the responsiveness of layer 5 neurons to inputs from outside of the local network.
source: Our results suggest that acetylcholine augments the responsiveness of layer 5 neurons to inputs from outside of the local network, possibly enabling faster switching between internal representations during locomotion.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings regarding layer 5 responses.

claim: Acetylcholine possibly enables faster switching between internal representations during locomotion.
source: Our results suggest that acetylcholine augments the responsiveness of layer 5 neurons to inputs from outside of the local network, possibly enabling faster switching between internal representations during locomotion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Acetylcholine gates experience-dependent changes in the responses of cortical neurons to sensory inputs.
source: A rich body of work has shown that acetylcholine gates experience-dependent changes in the responses of cortical neurons to sensory inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Acetylcholine gates receptive field plasticity in auditory cortex.
source: This includes receptive field plasticity in auditory cortex (Bakin et al., 1996; Froemke et al., 2007; Kilgard and Merzenich, 1998; Metherate and Weinberger, 1990)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Acetylcholine gates receptive field plasticity in somatosensory cortex.
source: This includes receptive field plasticity in auditory cortex (Bakin et al., 1996; Froemke et al., 2007; Kilgard and Merzenich, 1998; Metherate and Weinberger, 1990), somatosensory cortex (Ego-Stengel et al., 2001; Rasmusson and Dykes, 1988; Sachdev et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Acetylcholine gates receptive field plasticity in olfactory cortex.
source: This includes receptive field plasticity in auditory cortex (Bakin et al., 1996; Froemke et al., 2007; Kilgard and Merzenich, 1998; Metherate and Weinberger, 1990), somatosensory cortex (Ego-Stengel et al., 2001; Rasmusson and Dykes, 1988; Sachdev et al., 1998), and olfactory cortex (Wilson et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Acetylcholine gates ocular dominance plasticity in visual cortex.
source: or ocular dominance plasticity in visual cortex (Bear and Singer, 1986; Greuel et al., 1988; Gu and Singer, 1993; Kirkwood et al., 1999)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pairing of acetylcholine release with a sensory stimulus results in plasticity that increases the responsiveness of neurons to subsequent presentations of the same stimulus.
source: In all cases, the central tenet is that pairing of acetylcholine release or its application concurrent with a sensory stimulus results in plasticity that increases the responsiveness of neurons to subsequent presentations of the same stimulus.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the introduction based on prior research.

claim: Cholinergic projections to cortex arise from a population of neurons in the basal forebrain.
source: Cholinergic projections to cortex arise from a population of neurons in the basal forebrain (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: There is relatively broad functional heterogeneity within the population of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons.
source: Within this population of neurons, there is a relatively broad functional heterogeneity (Laszlovszky et al., 2020; Robert et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons show responses during movement including locomotion or licking.
source: Within this population of neurons, there is a relatively broad functional heterogeneity (Laszlovszky et al., 2020; Robert et al., 2021), with responses observed during movement – be it locomotion or licking (Harrison et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons show responses to reinforcers.
source: Within this population of neurons, there is a relatively broad functional heterogeneity (Laszlovszky et al., 2020; Robert et al., 2021), with responses observed during movement – be it locomotion or licking (Harrison et al., 2016), to reinforcers (Hangya et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons show responses to auditory stimuli.
source: Within this population of neurons, there is a relatively broad functional heterogeneity (Laszlovszky et al., 2020; Robert et al., 2021), with responses observed during movement – be it locomotion or licking (Harrison et al., 2016), to reinforcers (Hangya et al., 2015), to auditory stimuli (Guo et al., 2019; Robert et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons show weak responses to visual stimuli.
source: Within this population of neurons, there is a relatively broad functional heterogeneity (Laszlovszky et al., 2020; Robert et al., 2021), with responses observed during movement – be it locomotion or licking (Harrison et al., 2016), to reinforcers (Hangya et al., 2015), to auditory stimuli (Guo et al., 2019; Robert et al., 2021), and weakly to visual stimuli (Robert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Different regions in the basal forebrain project to different areas of cortex.
source: However, inferring acetylcholine release in specific cortical targets based on the activity of cholinergic neurons within the basal forebrain is complicated by the fact that different regions (Kim et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2013) and cholinergic cell types (Laszlovszky et al., 2020) in the basal forebrain project to different areas of cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Different cholinergic cell types in the basal forebrain project to different areas of cortex.
source: However, inferring acetylcholine release in specific cortical targets based on the activity of cholinergic neurons within the basal forebrain is complicated by the fact that different regions (Kim et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2013) and cholinergic cell types (Laszlovszky et al., 2020) in the basal forebrain project to different areas of cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Projection specificity likely underlies the heterogeneity in cholinergic activity across dorsal cortex.
source: This projection specificity likely underlies the heterogeneity in cholinergic activity across dorsal cortex (Collins et al., 2023; Lohani et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Movement in the form of a lever press is associated with cholinergic activity in mouse motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Measurements of cholinergic activity in cortex have found that movement in the form of a lever press is associated with cholinergic activity in mouse motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, and prefrontal cortex (Ren et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Whisking is associated with cholinergic axonal activity in barrel cortex.
source: Whisking is associated with cholinergic axonal activity in barrel cortex (Eggermann et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Sound is associated with cholinergic activity in auditory cortex.
source: while sound (Zhu et al., 2023) and movement (Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Zhu et al., 2023) are associated with cholinergic activity in auditory cortex
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Movement is associated with cholinergic activity in auditory cortex.
source: while sound (Zhu et al., 2023) and movement (Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Zhu et al., 2023) are associated with cholinergic activity in auditory cortex
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Locomotion is associated with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
source: and locomotion (Larsen et al., 2018; Lohani et al., 2022), facial movement (Lohani et al., 2022), and pupil dilation (Larsen et al., 2018; Reimer et al., 2016) are associated with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Facial movement is associated with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
source: and locomotion (Larsen et al., 2018; Lohani et al., 2022), facial movement (Lohani et al., 2022), and pupil dilation (Larsen et al., 2018; Reimer et al., 2016) are associated with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pupil dilation is associated with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
source: and locomotion (Larsen et al., 2018; Lohani et al., 2022), facial movement (Lohani et al., 2022), and pupil dilation (Larsen et al., 2018; Reimer et al., 2016) are associated with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cholinergic activity in cortex is closely related to movement.
source: Overall, cholinergic activity in cortex is closely related to movement, but whether movement is the primary determinant of cholinergic activity and how movement-related activity compares to sensory driven activity is less clear.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the introduction based on the cited literature.

claim: The primary functional effect of increased levels of acetylcholine in cortex is increased sensory responsiveness.
source: Likely the primary functional effect of increased levels of acetylcholine in cortex is increased sensory responsiveness.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Local application of acetylcholine increases sensory responses in somatosensory cortex in anesthetized cats.
source: Local application of acetylcholine has been shown to increase sensory responses in somatosensory cortex (Chatfield and Dempsey, 1942), auditory cortex (Forster and McCarter, 1946), as well as visual cortex (Sato et al., 1987) in anesthetized cats.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Local application of acetylcholine increases sensory responses in auditory cortex in anesthetized cats.
source: Local application of acetylcholine has been shown to increase sensory responses in somatosensory cortex (Chatfield and Dempsey, 1942), auditory cortex (Forster and McCarter, 1946), as well as visual cortex (Sato et al., 1987) in anesthetized cats.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Local application of acetylcholine increases sensory responses in visual cortex in anesthetized cats.
source: Local application of acetylcholine has been shown to increase sensory responses in somatosensory cortex (Chatfield and Dempsey, 1942), auditory cortex (Forster and McCarter, 1946), as well as visual cortex (Sato et al., 1987) in anesthetized cats.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Iontophoretic application of acetylcholine in rodent visual cortex induces a gain in visually evoked responses.
source: A similar gain in visually evoked responses in rodent visual cortex can be induced by iontophoretic application of acetylcholine in cortex (Sillito and Kemp, 1983)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Systemic acetylcholine release following basal forebrain stimulation induces a gain in visually evoked responses in rodent visual cortex.
source: A similar gain in visually evoked responses in rodent visual cortex can be induced by iontophoretic application of acetylcholine in cortex (Sillito and Kemp, 1983), by systemic acetylcholine release following basal forebrain stimulation (Goard and Dan, 2009; Pafundo et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic axons in visual cortex induces a gain in visually evoked responses.
source: A similar gain in visually evoked responses in rodent visual cortex can be induced by iontophoretic application of acetylcholine in cortex (Sillito and Kemp, 1983), by systemic acetylcholine release following basal forebrain stimulation (Goard and Dan, 2009; Pafundo et al., 2016), or by optogenetic stimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic axons in visual cortex (Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The increase of sensory responses caused by acetylcholine is not homogeneous across cortical layers.
source: Interestingly, this increase of sensory responses caused by acetylcholine is not homogeneous across cortical layers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Neurons responsive to iontophoretic application of acetylcholine are preferentially found in deep cortical layers.
source: Neurons responsive to iontophoretic application of acetylcholine are preferentially found in deep cortical layers (Krnjevic and Phillis, 1963).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The effects of acetylcholine are primarily one of facilitation of neuronal responses in deep cortical layers.
source: The effects of acetylcholine are primarily one of facilitation of neuronal responses in deep cortical layers and one of suppression in superficial layers (Sillito and Kemp, 1983; Soma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The effects of acetylcholine are primarily one of suppression in superficial cortical layers.
source: The effects of acetylcholine are primarily one of facilitation of neuronal responses in deep cortical layers and one of suppression in superficial layers (Sillito and Kemp, 1983; Soma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Local application of acetylcholine can result in selective hyperpolarization of layer 5 neurons.
source: However, depending on how locally acetylcholine is applied, it can also result in selective hyperpolarization of layer 5 neurons (Gulledge et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Nucleus basalis stimulation results in firing rate increases in layers 4, 5, and 6 of visual cortex.
source: Triggering systemic increase of acetylcholine by nucleus basalis stimulation results in firing rate increases in layers 4, 5, and 6 of visual cortex, but decreased firing rates in layer 2/3 (Goard and Dan, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Nucleus basalis stimulation results in decreased firing rates in layer 2/3 of visual cortex.
source: Triggering systemic increase of acetylcholine by nucleus basalis stimulation results in firing rate increases in layers 4, 5, and 6 of visual cortex, but decreased firing rates in layer 2/3 (Goard and Dan, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A direct layer-specific effect of acetylcholine on cortical processing would be consistent with differential expression of acetylcholine receptors across cortical layers.
source: While it is unclear whether the effect observed in the experiments that use systemic modulation of cholinergic activity is cortical or reflects a combination of changes in subcortical and cortical processing, a direct layer-specific effect on cortical processing would be consistent with differential expression of acetylcholine receptors across cortical layers (Obermayer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neuron stimulation desynchronizes activity in visual cortex.
source: Both basal forebrain cholinergic neuron stimulation and local cholinergic axon stimulation in visual cortex desynchronizes activity in visual cortex (Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Local cholinergic axon stimulation in visual cortex desynchronizes activity in visual cortex.
source: Both basal forebrain cholinergic neuron stimulation and local cholinergic axon stimulation in visual cortex desynchronizes activity in visual cortex (Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The decorrelation effect of acetylcholine is thought to be mediated by the influence of acetylcholine on somatostatin-positive interneurons and their interaction with excitatory neurons.
source: This effect is thought to be mediated by the influence of acetylcholine on somatostatin-positive interneurons and their interaction with the excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of somatostatin interneurons blocks acetylcholine-induced decorrelation.
source: This is based on the finding that optogenetic inhibition of somatostatin interneurons blocks acetylcholine-induced decorrelation (Chen et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Optogenetically induced acetylcholine release selectively enhances the input from excitatory neurons onto somatostatin interneurons.
source: and that optogenetically induced acetylcholine release selectively enhances the input from excitatory neurons onto somatostatin interneurons (Alitto and Dan, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Locomotion results in a decrease in correlation of neuronal activity in visual cortex.
source: A similar decrease in correlation has also been observed during locomotion (Aydın et al., 2018; Erisken et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The locomotion-induced decrease in correlation is stronger in deeper layers of cortex.
source: and the effect was stronger in deeper layers of cortex (Dadarlat and Stryker, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The decrease of correlations observed during locomotion may be driven by locomotion-related increases in acetylcholine.
source: It is possible that the decrease of correlations observed during locomotion is driven by locomotion-related increases in acetylcholine.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction.

claim: Locomotion modulates sensory evoked responses in visual cortex.
source: More generally, following the discovery of the modulation of sensory evoked responses by locomotion in visual cortex (Niell and Stryker, 2010), it has been speculated that acetylcholine is involved in locomotion-related changes in neuronal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A circuit projects from mesencephalic locomotor region to the basal forebrain, which when active, can bring about a gain of responses in visual cortex to visual stimuli.
source: Based on studies in rodents, a circuit was delineated that projects from mesencephalic locomotor region to the basal forebrain, which when active, can bring about a gain of responses in visual cortex to visual stimuli (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Nicotinic activation of VIP-expressing interneurons in visual cortex is necessary for locomotion-induced gain of visual responses.
source: It has been argued that nicotinic activation of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) expressing interneurons in visual cortex is necessary for this locomotion-induced gain of visual responses (Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: VIP interneurons are influenced by acetylcholine.
source: While VIP interneurons are clearly influenced by acetylcholine (Gasselin et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cholinergic receptors are expressed in all cortical cell types.
source: cholinergic receptors are expressed in all cortical cell types (Colangelo et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: There are likely direct functional effects of acetylcholine on many cortical cell types.
source: and there are likely direct functional effects of acetylcholine on many other cell types (Alitto and Dan, 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Gulledge and Stuart, 2005; Hay et al., 2016; Hedrick and Waters, 2015; Unal et al., 2012; Xiang et al., 1998; Zolles et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Most cortical cell types are likely directly influenced by acetylcholine.
source: This has called into question the interpretation that acetylcholine is involved in locomotion-related changes in neuronal activity primarily through nicotinic activation of VIP neurons - it is more likely that most cortical cell types are directly influenced (Pakan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic axons in visual cortex increase their activity on locomotion.
source: Nevertheless, all these lines of evidence come together to suggest that basal forebrain cholinergic axons in visual cortex increase their activity on locomotion and release acetylcholine to bring about a gain of visually evoked responses.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the introduction based on prior literature.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic axons release acetylcholine on locomotion to bring about a gain of visually evoked responses.
source: Nevertheless, all these lines of evidence come together to suggest that basal forebrain cholinergic axons in visual cortex increase their activity on locomotion and release acetylcholine to bring about a gain of visually evoked responses.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the introduction based on prior literature.

claim: The activity of many cholinergic axons strongly increased during locomotion.
source: We found that the activity in many cholinergic axons strongly increased during locomotion (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Cholinergic axon activity increased with locomotion onset.
source: Activity increased with locomotion onset (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The average lag of cholinergic axon activity increase relative to locomotion onset was 477 ms across all responsive axons.
source: with an average lag across all responsive axons of 477 ms relative to locomotion onset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Locomotion preceded the increase in cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
source: Thus, consistent with results reported for auditory cortex (Nelson and Mooney, 2016), we found that locomotion preceded the increase in cholinergic activity in visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the observed lag in cholinergic response.

claim: Locomotion onset results in an increase in activity of neurons in primary visual cortex.
source: Locomotion onset also results in an increase in activity of neurons in primary visual cortex (Ayaz et al., 2013; Keller et al., 2012; Saleem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The response latency of cholinergic axons was longer than the latency observed in responses of layer 2/3 neurons.
source: The response latency of cholinergic axons was longer than the latency we observed in responses of layer 2/3 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The response latency of cholinergic axons was shorter than that of layer 5 neurons.
source: but shorter than that of layer 5 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The initial increase in neuronal activity in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex was not driven by cholinergic input from basal forebrain.
source: This would suggest that the initial increase in neuronal activity in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex was not driven by cholinergic input from basal forebrain.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the latency comparison.

claim: 52.3% ± 4.4% (mean ± SEM) of cholinergic axons responded significantly to locomotion onset.
source: For each imaging site, we then quantified the percentage of cholinergic axons that exhibited significant responses to locomotion onset, full field drifting gratings, or visuomotor mismatch, and found that 52.3% ± 4.4% (mean ± SEM) of the axons responded significantly to locomotion onset
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the Results section.

claim: The fraction of cholinergic axons responsive to gratings was not different from chance.
source: while the fraction of responsive axons to gratings and mismatch was not different from chance (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The fraction of cholinergic axons responsive to visuomotor mismatch was not different from chance.
source: while the fraction of responsive axons to gratings and mismatch was not different from chance (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: An increase in calcium activity in cholinergic axons corresponds to an increase in extracellular acetylcholine.
source: To confirm that an increase in calcium activity in cholinergic axons corresponds to an increase in extracellular acetylcholine, we measured acetylcholine levels using the genetically-encoded acetylcholine sensor GRAB-Ach3.0 (Jing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and confirmed by GRAB-ACh measurements.

claim: Acetylcholine levels in visual cortex increased on locomotion onsets.
source: We found that consistent with the calcium activity of cholinergic axons, acetylcholine levels in visual cortex increased on locomotion onsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Grating onsets resulted in no measurable increase in acetylcholine levels when corrected for hemodynamic artifacts.
source: while grating onsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and visuomotor mismatches (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) resulted in no measurable increase when corrected for hemodynamic artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Visuomotor mismatches resulted in no measurable increase in acetylcholine levels when corrected for hemodynamic artifacts.
source: while grating onsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and visuomotor mismatches (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) resulted in no measurable increase when corrected for hemodynamic artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Locomotion is associated with a basal forebrain-driven increase in acetylcholine levels in visual cortex.
source: Thus, consistent with previous reports (Larsen et al., 2018), we find that locomotion is associated with a basal forebrain-driven increase in acetylcholine levels in visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the GRAB-ACh data and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Cholinergic axon activity was not linearly related to locomotion velocity.
source: Further characterizing the relationship between locomotion velocity and cholinergic activity, we found that cholinergic axon activity was not linearly related to locomotion velocity, but instead exhibited a locomotion state dependence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Cholinergic axon activity exhibited a locomotion state dependence.
source: Further characterizing the relationship between locomotion velocity and cholinergic activity, we found that cholinergic axon activity was not linearly related to locomotion velocity, but instead exhibited a locomotion state dependence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Velocity decreased systematically over the course of a locomotion bout.
source: Over the course of a locomotion bout, we found that velocity decreased systematically, such that towards the end of a locomotion bout, velocity was lower than at the beginning (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no evidence of a difference in the average calcium activity of cholinergic axons after locomotion onset to that before locomotion offset.
source: We found no evidence of a difference in the average calcium activity of cholinergic axons after locomotion onset to that before locomotion offset (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average cholinergic activity after locomotion onset and before locomotion offset was highly correlated across locomotion bouts.
source: Indeed, the average cholinergic activity after locomotion onset and before locomotion offset was highly correlated across locomotion bouts
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The time-course of locomotion velocity is more variable and less correlated bout-by-bout than cholinergic activity.
source: while a similar analysis on locomotion velocity revealed that the time-course of velocity is more variable and less correlated bout-by-bout (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The activity after locomotion onset, before locomotion offset, and the average activity during the locomotion bout were all well correlated on an axon-by-axon level.
source: The similarity of locomotion onset and offset responses was not only true for the population average activity, but the activity after locomotion onset, before locomotion offset, and the average activity during the locomotion bout were all well correlated on an axon-by-axon level (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The relationship between locomotion velocity and calcium activity in cholinergic axons was more step-like than linear.
source: To quantify the relationship between locomotion velocity and calcium activity in cholinergic axons more generally, we computed the average calcium activity as a function of locomotion velocity (see Methods). This relationship was more step-like than linear
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: There was no evidence of an increase in calcium activity in cholinergic axons between low and high locomotion velocities.
source: and we found no evidence of an increase in calcium activity between low and high locomotion velocities (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Calcium activity in cholinergic axons correlates better with a binarized version of locomotion velocity than with locomotion velocity itself.
source: If calcium activity in cholinergic axons reflected a step-like change during locomotion, we should find that calcium activity correlates better with a binarized version of locomotion velocity than with locomotion velocity itself. This is indeed what we found (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Calcium activity in cholinergic axons in visual cortex is better described as a binary locomotion state signal than a linear locomotion velocity signal.
source: Thus, calcium activity in cholinergic axons in visual cortex is better described as a binary locomotion state signal, than a linear locomotion velocity signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the analysis of the relationship between cholinergic activity and locomotion velocity.

claim: The correlation of locomotion velocity and cholinergic activity was independent of visuomotor condition.
source: This analysis was motivated by our observation that average light levels have a stronger influence on pupil size than locomotion state. We found that the correlation of locomotion velocity and cholinergic activity was independent of visuomotor condition (Figure 3A).

claim: The correlation between pupil diameter and cholinergic activity was lower during closed loop visuomotor coupling than during open loop or grating conditions.

claim: The reduced correlation between locomotion velocity and pupil diameter in darkness was not a consequence of a decrease in variability due to ceiling-effects in pupil diameter in darkness.

claim: The correlation of cholinergic activity with locomotion was higher than that with facial movements under all conditions tested.

claim: Of locomotion, pupil diameter, and facial movements, locomotion exhibited the most robust correlation with cholinergic activity in visual cortex.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: During locomotion, visual responses in visual cortex are increased.

One of these effects is that during locomotion, visual responses in visual cortex are increased (Niell and Stryker, 2010) through a combination of both additive and multiplicative effects (Dadarlat and Stryker, 2017).

claim: Locomotion-driven increases in visual responses are apparent in both layer 2/3 and layer 5 neurons.

claim: Acetylcholine could function to gate visuomotor plasticity to phases of self-motion.
source: Given our results, what are the implications for the computational role of acetylcholine in visual cortex? There are likely two aspects to this, the acute effect on cortical activity and the effect on plasticity. We find that acetylcholine was released in visual cortex as a locomotion state signal. This state signal could be used to gate visuomotor plasticity. In systems engaged in sensorimotor learning, plasticity related to feedback prediction errors should occur primarily during self-motion and not when passively experiencing sensory input. Visuomotor development is critically dependent on coupling of locomotion and sensory feedback (Attinger et al., 2017; Held and Hein, 1963; Kaneko and Stryker, 2014), and depends on local plasticity mechanisms in visual cortex (Widmer et al., 2022). Acetylcholine is known to gate plasticity in visual cortex (Bear and Singer, 1986; Greuel et al., 1988; Gu and Singer, 1993; Kirkwood et al., 1999) and could function to gate visuomotor plasticity to phases of self-motion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings and prior literature.

claim: Visuomotor development is critically dependent on coupling of locomotion and sensory feedback.
source: Visuomotor development is critically dependent on coupling of locomotion and sensory feedback (Attinger et al., 2017; Held and Hein, 1963; Kaneko and Stryker, 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Visuomotor development depends on local plasticity mechanisms in visual cortex.
source: and depends on local plasticity mechanisms in visual cortex (Widmer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Acetylcholine could function more generally as a movement state signal.
source: Given that acetylcholine release is associated with other types of movement as well (Eggermann et al., 2014; Harrison et al., 2016; Lohani et al., 2022; Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Zhu et al., 2023), this is consistent with acetylcholine functioning more generally as a movement state signal.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings and prior literature.

claim: Locomotion-driven neuronal activity in visual cortex is likely not driven by acetylcholine, but is the consequence of a combination of motor-related top-down input and noradrenaline.
source: The absence of an acute effect of optogenetically stimulating cholinergic axons locally on the activity of visual cortex neurons is consistent with the idea that locomotion-driven neuronal activity in visual cortex (Keller et al., 2012; Saleem et al., 2013) is likely not driven by acetylcholine, but is the consequence of a combination of motor-related top-down input (Leinweber et al., 2017) and noradrenaline (Polack et al., 2013), another neuromodulator that is known to accompany locomotion onset (Jordan and Keller, 2023; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings and prior literature.

claim: Acetylcholine acutely increases visuomotor responses more strongly in layer 5 neurons than in layer 2/3 neurons.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Goard and Dan, 2009), we find that acetylcholine acutely increases visuomotor responses more strongly in layer 5 neurons than in layer 2/3 neurons and that it decorrelates neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Acetylcholine decorrelates neuronal activity.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Goard and Dan, 2009), we find that acetylcholine acutely increases visuomotor responses more strongly in layer 5 neurons than in layer 2/3 neurons and that it decorrelates neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The observed effects of acetylcholine on layer 5 can be explained by assuming the layer 5 network exhibits attractor dynamics and that acetylcholine modifies these attractor dynamics.
source: We propose a slightly more specific explanation. This is based on the idea that the observed effects of acetylcholine on layer 5 can be explained by assuming the layer 5 network exhibits attractor dynamics and that acetylcholine modifies these attractor dynamics (Kanamaru and Aihara, 2019).
